He named them *al-'Asifat* because they rush swiftly, as winds do, in carrying out God's commands. He named them *al-Nashirat* because they spread their wings in the air, and because they spread the laws (shara'i') on earth, or spread the records of deeds. He named them *al-Fariqat* because they distinguish between truth and falsehood. He named them *al-Nashirat* because they spread the clouds in the sky, as in His saying: ﴿He sends the winds, and they stir up clouds﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. He named them *al-Fariqat* because they separate the clouds, as in His saying: ﴿and makes it into fragments﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. As for ﴿fa-al-Mulqiyat dhikran﴾ (﴿then those who convey a reminder﴾), they are the angels, because they convey the reminder to the prophets, peace be upon them.

The more apparent view regarding *al-Nashirat* and *al-Fariqat* is that they are the angels, because the description of *al-Fariqat* fits them better than the winds. Also, *al-Mulqiyat* mentioned after them are the angels, and no one has said they are the winds. For this reason, He joined the homogeneous items (al-mutajanisayn, i.e., items of the same kind) with *fa-* (then), saying *wa-al-Mursalat fa-al-'Asifat*, and then joined an item that is not of the same kind with *wa-* (and), saying *wa-al-Nashirat*, and then joined the homogeneous items to it with *fa-*. It has been said that *al-Mursalat* and *al-Mulqiyat* are the prophets, peace be upon them.

*'Urfan* (عُرْفاً) means bounty and kindness. It is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih). It is possible that both are verbal nouns, in which case their accusative case is by substitution (badal) from *dhikran*, or as an object of *dhikr* (as an object governed by a verb of meaning related to dhikr). It is also possible that *'udhran* is the plural of *'adhir* or *'adhir*, and *nudhran* is the plural of *nadhir*, in which case their accusative case is circumstantial (hal).

*Innama tu'adduna la-waqi'* (﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾) means the resurrection and the recompense, and this is the answer to the oath.

Al-A'sha al-Tamimi read the dhal with a damma (ضم) in both places, while the rest of the readers read it with a sukun (إسكان). It is possible that both are verbal nouns, in which case their accusative case is by substitution (badal) from *dhikran*, or as an object of *dhikr* (as an object governed by a verb of meaning related to dhikr). It is also possible that *'udhran* is the plural of *'adhir* or *'adhir*, and *nudhran* is the plural of *nadhir*, in which case their accusative case is circumstantial (hal).

*Innama tu'adduna la-waqi'* (﴿What you are promised will surely occur﴾) means the resurrection and the recompense, and this is the answer to the oath.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 77, verses 8–15:

﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾, i.e., their light disappears; it was also said: they are erased. ﴿And when the sky is split open﴾, i.e., it is cleft asunder. ﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾, i.e., they become dust. ﴿And when the messengers are brought to their appointed time﴾, i.e., a known time is set for them, so that time arrives and they are gathered to bear witness against their nations on the Day of Resurrection. Abu 'Amr read ﴿wuqqitat﴾ with a waw, which is the original form, and the hamza is a substitution for the waw. ﴿For what day were they postponed?﴾ It is from the root "ajal" (term, appointed time), just as "tawqit" (fixing a time) is from "waqt" (time). In it is a kind of emphasis intended to magnify that day. Then he explained it with His words: ﴿For the Day of Judgment (Yawm al-Fasl)﴾, i.e., the day on which judgment is passed between the servants. Then He magnified it with His words: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Judgment is? Woe on that day to the deniers﴾. Its repetition in this surah: it was said that it is an emphasis; and it was also said: rather, in every verse there is something that calls for affirmation, so "Woe on that day to the deniers" comes back to what precedes it in each place within it.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 77, verses 16–18:

﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ Meaning the earlier disbelievers, such as the people of Noah and others. ﴿Then We follow them with the later ones.﴾ Meaning Quraysh and others among the disbelievers who rejected Muhammad (ﷺ). Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 77, verse 20–23:

﴿Did We not create you from a despised fluid?﴾ It means the semen (al-maniy), and al-maheen means weak. ﴿Then We placed it in a firm place﴾ meaning the womb of the woman. ﴿For a known period﴾ meaning the time of birth, which is known to be nine months, or less or more than that. ﴿Then We determined⁠—﴾ with the doubled letter (qaddarna, from al-taqdir, "determination") and without it (qadarna, from al-qudrah, "power"). If it is from power, it agrees with His words, ﴿So We are the best of those who determine⁠—﴾ [or: "the best of those who have power"]. And if it is from determination, then it is a paronomasia (tajnis).

Qur'anic quotations: ﴿أَلَمْ نَجْعَلِ ٱلأَرْضَ كِفَاتاً * أَحْيَآءً وَأَمْواتاً﴾ 

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 77, verse 25–27:

﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle, for the living and the dead?﴾ Al-kifat (receptacle) is from kafata, meaning when one gathers and collects something together. The meaning is that the earth gathers the living upon its surface and the dead within its belly. The words aḥyā'an wa-amwātan (for the living and the dead) are in the accusative because they are the object of kifātan, since kifāt is a noun meaning that which gathers and collects; it is as if He said: "gathering the living and the dead." It is also permissible that the meaning is: it gathers them, living and dead, so that their accusative case is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun. The words aḥyā'an and amwātan are indefinite for the sake of magnification and to indicate their great number.

﴿Rawasiya (firm mountains)﴾ means the mountains, that is, lofty ones. ﴿Shamikhat (towering)﴾ ﴿And We gave you sweet water to drink﴾ meaning fresh (sweet) water.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 77, verses 29–33:

﴿Inṭalaqū﴾ (Depart!) is addressed to the deniers. Yaʿqub read the lām with a fatḥa, making it a past-tense verb, and then repeated it to clarify the destination to which they depart. ﴿To a shadow﴾: meaning the smoke of Hell, and from it is the shadow of yahmum (scorching black smoke). ﴿Of three branches﴾: meaning three branches stem from the smoke, which shade them, whereas the believers are in the shades of the Throne. It has also been said that this verse refers to the worshippers of the cross, because they are (divided) into three branches, so it is said to them: "Depart to it." ﴿Neither cooling nor protecting﴾: it negates that it shades them as the Throne shades the believers, and it also negates that it keeps the flame away from them. ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a fortress﴾: the pronoun in "indeed it" refers to Hell. Qaṣr (fortress) is the singular of qusūr, meaning great dwellings. The sparks are likened to them in their magnitude and in their height in the air. It has also been said that qaṣr is a thick tree, its singular being qaṣrah, like jamrah and jamr (ember and embers). ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾: concerning the word jimālāt (camels) there are two opinions. The first: it is the plural of jamāl (camel), and the sparks are likened to them, with ṣufr (yellow) taken in its apparent sense, because the color of fire tends toward yellow. It has also been said that ṣufr here means black, as in the saying "a jamal aṣfar," meaning a black camel. This is more fitting to the description of Hell. The second: that jimālāt are the large pieces of copper, so it is as if the word is derived from jumlah (a mass). It was also read as jumālāt with a ḍammah on the jīm, meaning the great ropes of ships, namely their large cables.

Qaṣr (fortress) is the singular of qusūr, meaning great dwellings. The sparks are likened to them in their magnitude and in their height in the air. It has also been said that qaṣr is a thick tree, its singular being qaṣrah, like jamrah and jamr (ember and embers). ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾: concerning the word jimālāt (camels) there are two opinions. The first: it is the plural of jamāl (camel), and the sparks are likened to them, with ṣufr (yellow) taken in its apparent sense, because the color of fire tends toward yellow. It has also been said that ṣufr here means black, as in the saying "a jamal aṣfar," meaning a black camel. This is more fitting to the description of Hell. The second: that jimālāt are the large pieces of copper, so it is as if the word is derived from jumlah (a mass). It was also read as jumālāt with a ḍammah on the jīm, meaning the great ropes of ships, namely their large cables.

This is the day when they will not speak. This refers to certain occasions, and they may speak on other occasions, as in His saying: ﴿On the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself﴾ [al-Nahl: 111].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 77, verse 39:

﴿So if you have a plot, then plot against Me.﴾ A challenge to them (*ta'jīz*, rendering them incapable), an allusion to their scheming in the world, and a rebuke for it.

Eat and drink with ease (hanî'an) for what you used to do. This is said to them in Paradise, either through the tongue of circumstance (bi-lisan al-hal) or through the tongue of speech (bi-lisan al-maqal). "Hanî'an" is in the accusative, either as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal) or as an object of supplication (du'a').

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 77, verse 46:

﴿Eat and enjoy yourselves [for a little while]﴾ is an address to the disbelievers in the form of a threat. Its implied sense is: say to them, "Eat and enjoy yourselves a little in this world."

And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down. This is a report about the state of the disbelievers in this world. Mention of bowing (rukuʿ) stands for prayer (ṣalāh). It has also been said that the meaning of "bow down" is "humble yourselves and be humbly submissive." It has also been said that this is a report about the state of the hypocrites on the Day of Resurrection, because when it is said to them, "Bow down," they will be unable to bow, like the words of Allah: ﴿And they will be called to prostration, but they will not be able to do it﴾ [al-Qalam: 42]. The first view is the more well-known and the more evident.
﴿So in what statement after it will they believe?﴾ The pronoun refers to the Qur'an.
